speaker: Dean Kassmann, SVP of Engineering & Technology, IonQ
verdict_reasoning:
Evidence gathered from the pre-registered resolver sources only. The tracked target, as stated in IonQ's July 2024 roadmap announcement, was 99.999% (“five nines”) LOGICAL two-qubit gate fidelity using small-distance quantum error-correcting codes, by the end of 2025.

Inside the window (31 Dec 2025 plus the 30-day grace, i.e. by 30 Jan 2026) IonQ did publish a two-qubit gate result: on 20–21 October 2025 it reported a gate error of 8.4(7)×10⁻⁵ — about 99.9916% fidelity — using Electronic Qubit Control without ground-state cooling, demonstrated on prototype systems in IonQ's R&D labs (arXiv:2510.17286; IonQ newsroom; The Quantum Insider, 21 Oct 2025). That is a PHYSICAL (native) gate fidelity. No error-correcting code is involved, and it is measured on prototype hardware rather than a deployed system. It is a real advance, it was reported as a world record on the physical axis, and it comfortably clears the same roadmap's separate >99.9% native target — but it is not the claim tracked here. No result at or above 99.999% logical two-qubit gate fidelity with small-distance QEC codes appears in any named resolver source inside the window.

On the PARTIALLY_VERIFIED branch, recorded so the reading is auditable rather than assumed: the criteria offer that branch for “a result close to but short of five nines (e.g. four nines) … reported as the headline achievement instead.” The desk reads it as scoped to LOGICAL fidelity, because the sentence immediately before it forbids conflating the native figure with the logical one. A four-nines PHYSICAL result is a different measurement, not a near miss on the same one, so the branch does not fire.

This is a statement about a dated claim and its deadline, not about the people who made it.
